item.title: House Democrats plan ambitious 100-day agenda if they sweep to power in midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats are preparing an ambitious 100-days agenda focused on delivering their campaign promises — making life more affordable and conducting vast oversight of the Trump administration — if the party seizes majority control in next month's elections . Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries , who is in line to become House speaker if the party wins power, said the Democrats will be united "right out of the gate" on reinstating Affordable Care Act tax breaks , reversing Republican Medicaid cuts, holding votes against the Iran war and undoing President Donald Trump's tariff regime . They expect to launch the agenda in the first 100 hours, once the new Congress is seated in January. "Fighting for an affordable America — that's what unites Democrats all across the country," Jeffries said recently at the party campaign headquarters in Washington. "That's our commitment to the American people, because the cost of living is way too high and far too many people who are working hard, playing by the rules, can't thrive and can barely survive — and are drowning — in the Trump economy." It's a hyper-focused agenda tapping into the voter sentiment that is driving much of the midterm election as Americans wrestle with affordability concerns and inflationary costs from the Iran war and other policies. The undertaking will also test the ability of the sprawling House Democrats to work together and avoid the chaotic divisions and disruptions that have hobbled Republicans under Speaker Mike Johnson's leadership. Democrats have been out of power in the House since 2023. If Jeffries takes the helm, he would be the first Democratic speaker since Nancy Pelosi , leading a new generation of lawmakers that includes a handful of far-left candidates who are aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America . "The antidote to that is getting things done," said Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski, who is poised to become chair of the New Democrat Coalition, the largest caucus within the House Democrats. She said the party is determined to show the American people that "Democrats know how to govern." A Freedom Caucus of the far-left? Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said he is often asked if Democrats will be confronting their own version of the Freedom Caucus, referring to the far-right Republicans who often grind the House agenda to a halt. "It doesn't work that way," Casar told The Associated Press in an interview. "The Freedom Caucus breaks things. But if you're a progressive, you want to pass things." Leader Jeffries, Casar and other Democrats have been in touch with the progressive candidates, many of whom are backed by the DSA as the party focuses on shared priorities. "This notion that because we'll have new members somehow we're going to be disjointed — not so," said Louisiana Rep. Troy Carter, who hopes to become chair of the Congressional Black Caucus. "All those banking on that, save the popcorn for another day." The Republicans, who are confronting an increasingly difficult election-year climate to hold onto their majority, portray Democrats as beholden to a far-left socialist agenda. If Republicans retain power, Johnson has said they would press on with what they have already accomplished alongside Trump, which has been an agenda focused on cutting taxes and federal spending. "What we would do in the next two years is exactly what we have been doing already," Johnson said on CNBC's Squawk Box, "and that is putting the conditions in place for a strong America again." Fix healthcare, stop the war, end the tariffs – and investigate Trump Months ago, Jeffries launched five working groups to tackle the affordability agenda focused on healthcare, housing, groceries and goods, gas and utilities, and care-giving. Each group is headed by a progressive and a centrist Democrat — the healthcare working group, for example, is run by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama — with the goal of striking common ground on draft policies that all House Democrats can support. At the same time, Jeffries has tasked the ranking Democrats on the House Oversight and Judiciary committees with preparing investigations. They are focused on Trump, his family and his administration, as part of a sweeping anti-corruption agenda. Impeachment , Jeffries has said, is neither on nor off the table. "We need to lower the cost of groceries and gas. Two, we need to make healthcare affordable for every single American. Three, we're going to hold the crooks accountable who've visited unprecedented corruption on the American people," Jeffries said. "Beginning on day one." Democrats plan to vote quickly to reinstate the health care tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, which expired in 2025, leaving millions of Americans confronting higher health insurance costs. Proposals are also ready to reverse the Medicaid cuts that Republicans put in place as part of their "One Big Beautiful Bill" of tax breaks and program cuts, including new work requirements for recipients. There are measures to reverse Trump's tariffs as Congress works to claw back power from the White House. And Democrats, who have forced multiple votes on ending the Iran conflict, plan to pressure the Trump administration to end the military action by pushing forward more war powers resolutions. Much of the House Democrats' agenda, if they regain power, would depend on the size of the majority. Details also depend on the Senate, and whether it flips to Democrats. "We cannot simply go back to the status quo," said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesman for Justice Democrats, an outside group that supports the far-left progressives. And Trump, at the White House, has ultimate say, with veto power at the stroke of a pen. "We're going to do a lot and we're going to be very busy," Carter said. "We will not be able to fix everything overnight." This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/house-democrats-plan-first-100-041403400.html

item.title: Can Trump strip Ilhan Omar of her U.S. citizenship? It's not that simple.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Democrat from Minnesota, during a news conference at the US Capitol on Feb. 24, 2026, in Washington, D.C. —Daniel Heuer—Bloomberg via Getty Images In a highly unusual step, federal agents this week aggressively intensified their investigations into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, weeks before she stands for reelection in her home district. The Department of Justice on Tuesday subpoenaed relatives of Omar’s family members, including her sister Sahra Noor, according to The New York Times . The grand jury subpoenas were issued shortly after a raid of the lawmaker’s residence in Washington, D.C. on Monday. The judicial search warrant, which is under seal, was executed by Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement . Although the Department of Justice did not provide any more details of the investigation, multiple outlets , citing anonymous sources, reported that the search stemmed from Omar’s immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child. Prior to the investigation, multiple Trump Administration officials have accused Omar of immigration fraud without presenting any evidence. In a podcast interview in March, Vice President JD Vance said the White House was exploring “legal remedies” to her alleged immigration fraud. Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the investigation into Omar was “ongoing” and dismissed efforts to frame the case as political retribution. “If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said during the interview with right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson. Omar, who has long denied the allegations, condemned the raid on her home as “political intimidation” and said she will “not be silenced.” President Trump, along with many MAGA Republicans, has repeatedly floated the idea of revoking Omar’s citizenship, a process also known as denaturalization, and deporting her. But legal and immigration experts tell TIME that denaturalizing a U.S. citizen is a rare and difficult process, one that requires federal authorities to clear a high bar in front of a federal judge. Here’s what to know about how the process works. How does denaturalization work? Stripping someone of their citizenship is a more arduous legal process than most other immigration efforts that involve the courts. Deportation proceedings, for instance, are initiated by ICE agents under the Department of Homeland Security and are then approved by immigration judges who are hired and work within the Department of Justice. The denaturalization process, on the other hand, must be approved by an independent federal judge, who evaluates the request by a higher standard. All denaturalization efforts begin at DOJ. In order to revoke a naturalized person’s citizenship, a DOJ lawyer must decide whether to file a civil or a criminal petition in court. Yuripzy Morgan, an attorney and host of Free Range National podcase, said a civil complaint does not have a statute of limitation, whereas a criminal complaint has a statute of limitation of 10 years and must clear a much higher legal bar. “For civil denaturalization, the government has to show that there is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence that the person in question obtained their naturalization either illegally, or they willfully misrepresented a material fact, ” Morgan says. She stressed that simply having an error in an immigration document doesn't mean that a judge is going to approve stripping a person of their citizenship. For a criminal denaturalization conviction, the federal government must show “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” that the individual knowingly obtained citizenship through fraud, which is the highest legal standard of proof required to secure a criminal conviction. In 2017, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in Maslenjak v. United States that only an illegal act that played a role in a person’s citizenship application could lead to criminal denaturalization, further narrowing down the scope of such efforts. Omar’s father filled out and submitted her citizenship application on her behalf when she was 17. It is unclear what evidence, if any, the federal government has to show that anything in the application was fraudulent, or that Omar or her father intentionally misrepresented anything in that application. Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge and a resident fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, pointed out that even after someone gets denaturalized, a deportation is not guaranteed. The person would still be able to retain their previous legal immigration status until a final order of removal is issued to the person by ICE. “If they had a green card before they naturalized, even after they get denaturalized, they are going to have a green card,” Arthur says. How did Rep. Omar get naturalized as a U.S. citizen? According to Omar’s House biography, Omar and her family fled her home country Somalia when she was eight. The family eventually sought asylum in the United States in 1995. She told The New York Times that she became a U.S. citizen in 2000 when she was 17. At the time Omar went through the process, federal law allowed immigrants under the age of 18 to get naturalized as U.S. citizens if both of their parents had become U.S. citizens. The law was eventually replaced by a new law in 2001, which only requires one parent to become a citizen for the children to be naturalized. At the center of this investigation is whether Omar’s father, Nur Omar Mohamed, lied about her age in immigration documents so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him, according to The Washington Post , which cited two unnamed sources. According to Arthur, the former immigration judge, if Omar was 18 at the time of the naturalization application, she may have been able to apply for her citizenship on her own after having a valid green card for five years. The allegations regarding Omar’s citizenship gained attention among conservative activists and commentators starting in 2019, when Omar became a member of Congress. Shortly after her election, Omar’s staff sought to change her official birth year in public records from 1981 to 1982, according to multiple outlets . How often does the U.S. government strip people of their citizenship? Despite the renewed push from the second Trump administration, denaturalization remains an exceedingly rare legal process. According to the Migration Policy Institute , a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, an average of 11 denaturalization cases were filed per year between 1990 and 2017. Denaturalization efforts have increased in Trump’s second term. The DOJ has announced efforts to strip at least 108 people of their citizenship in 2026. That is still considerably smaller than the hundreds of thousands of people whom the U.S. government grants citizenship to through naturalization every year. This article originally appeared on Time at https://time.com/article/2026/10/14/ilhan-omar-citizenship-investigation-denaturalization-DOJ/

item.title: Jon Ossoff shuts down 2028 presidential speculation in heated Georgia Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Mike Collins listens to Sen. Jon Ossoff during a debate Tuesday. (Mike Stewart / AP) Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said Tuesday night during a debate that he will not run for president in 2028. Ossoff made the statement in response to a question as he faced off with his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is seeking a second six-year term in Georgia and said he would serve the full term. “I have zero interest in running for president,” Ossoff said when he was asked directly by one of the moderators. “I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate.” Ossoff has been regularly discussed as a potential Democratic contender in 2028. If he were to win the presidency, he would have to give up his Senate seat, which he stressed Tuesday night that he would not do. After the brief remark, Ossoff quickly transitioned to pressing Collins about why he has supported President Donald Trump’s tariffs, a main focus of both his campaign and a debate the two held last week . Tuesday was the second debate in the nationally watched Georgia Senate race, this one organized by the Atlanta Press Club. Collins quipped that Ossoff was actually trying to run for president and will be “your DSA candidate,” a reference to the Democratic Socialists of America. The exchange came at the beginning of the hourlong debate, which covered ground including data centers; the economy under Trump, whose approval rating is at record lows; the war in Iran; and the issue of Collins’ son-in-law’s promoting white nationalist posts on social media. Ossoff asked Collins directly whether he considered himself a “white nationalist.” “I condemn any sort of hate speech,” Collins said. “Antisemitism, hate of any kind. It’s abhorrent.” The exchange continued when Collins again asked Ossoff to denounce Reid Hoffman, a major donor to Democratic causes — including Ossoff-aligned political committees — whose name appeared in the Epstein files . Collins brought up Hoffman several times last week and did so again during the second debate. Ossoff did not directly respond, and he again pointed to the fact that those close to Collins amplified white nationalists’ posts. “How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for Senate?” Ossoff said. “The paper reported it’s still going on today.” Given a chance to respond, Collins did not address it directly. But he said rhetoric like Ossoff’s had motivated a New York man who is accused of making death threats against him. “I’m a little tired of this, Jon,” Collins said. “This crazy person is in jail right now because of your rhetoric.” Neither candidate directly answered the other’s charges. Collins also, once again, did not answer questions about whether or not Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. He was asked about audio of a call Trump made after the 2020 election asking Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “ find 11,780 votes ” to help overturn the 2020 election. “You know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it,” Collins said. This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/heated-georgia-senate-debate-jon-ossoff-says-wont-run-president-2028-rcna603300

item.title: Zelensky says Trump is abandoning a key partner while easing pressure on Russia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
On Saturday, Donald Trump said Ukraine needed a new leader - AFP via Getty Images/BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI Volodymyr Zelensky said that he felt betrayed by Donald Trump, and warned the US president was not acting on the “right side of history”. “It is a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” the Ukrainian leader said on Wednesday amid an escalating public clash with his American counterpart. Relations between Kyiv and the White House have sharply deteriorated after Mr Trump agreed on Friday to waive sanctions on Russia to import diesel . The US president has been pressuring Ukraine to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming Kyiv – not the Iran war – for rising energy prices. On Saturday he said Ukraine needed “a new president” . In an interview with Piers Morgan Uncensored, scheduled to air on Wednesday, Mr Zelensky said he would not resign under US pressure. Asked whether he felt “betrayed” by recent events, he said: “Really, yes, between us. But it’s a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings. “Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump. They wanted us not to attack. My opinion was, it is not fair.” ‘People will die’ The US has also threatened to suspend intelligence-sharing to force Ukraine to stop its refinery attacks. Mr Zelensky claimed on Tuesday that Kyiv had stopped receiving warnings from allies about missile attacks. He also accused Elon Musk, the tech billionaire, of imposing limits on his Starlink technology, which are critical communication devices for Ukrainian forces on the front line. “I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Mr Zelensky said. Addressing Mr Musk directly, he added: “This decision will bring a lot of human losses. Of course, people will die.” Mr Zelensky told Piers Morgan that he would not resign under US pressure Nato, EU and Ukrainian officials have told The Telegraph that they have seen no signs that US intelligence-sharing has stopped with the country. The US has not commented on the matter and Kyiv is still waiting to hear from the Trump administration, a Ukrainian official familiar with discussions told The Telegraph. Kyiv maintains it has not hit any oil refineries since Mr Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday . During Wednesday’s visit to the UK, Mr Zelensky also pressed Andy Burnham to use the proceeds of Roman Abramovich’s sale of Chelsea Football Club to support Ukraine. Ahead of their Downing Street meeting, sources said the Ukrainian president would argue that the £2.5bn funds were needed to offset the damage done by Mr Trump’s diesel deal with Vladimir Putin. Mr Zelensky also pushed Mr Burnham to confiscate frozen Russian assets held in Britain to ratchet up the economic pressure on Moscow. The EU failed last year to reach a decision on the seizure of some €210bn (£183bn) in Russian state bank assets being held on the Continent, mainly in Belgium. Sir Keir Starmer, the then prime minister, used the failure to back down on a promise to do the same. Mr Burnham said he would seek to ‘repair bridges’ between Kyiv and Washington in his meetings with Mr Zelensky - REUTERS/Corey Rudy Britain has been locked in a dispute with Mr Abramovich, who has close ties to Putin, about the use of the proceeds of the Chelsea sale. The Russian oligarch was sanctioned by the Government following the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Ministers eventually allowed the billionaire to sell the football club based on the condition that the money would go to “victims of the war in Ukraine”. Mr Abramovich has since set up the Foundation for the Victims of Conflict to oversee the dispersal of the funds . But his organisation has disagreed with the Government about whether the money can be spent on humanitarian causes across a range of countries. After months without an update, Ukrainian officials put the issue on Mr Zelensky’s agenda to raise with Mr Burnham during their meeting. Mr Zelensky also met the King at Buckingham Palace and thanked him for his support - Aaron Chown/Reuters Before the talks, the Prime Minister told the House of Commons that he would seek to mend relations between Kyiv and Washington. Speaking in the Commons, Mr Burnham told MPs: “What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back. “Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together. That is the role I intend to play.” Mr Zelensky also met the King at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday afternoon. In a social media post, the Ukrainian president said: “I thank the King, the Prime Minister, and all of Britain for their support!” After his meetings in London, he will travel to hold talks with European leaders at a summit in Brussels. This article originally appeared on The Telegraph at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/zelensky-feel-betrayed-trump-173810626.html

item.title: Social Security benefits are getting their biggest boost since 2023. But there's a catch.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Social Security and SSI benefits will increase by 3.6% in 2027 for more than 72 million people, the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced today. The cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is the biggest since 2023 and means, on average, retirement benefits will rise by $75 a month, SSA said. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) says that works out to roughly $900 a year, and estimates the highest earners will see an increase of more than $2,200 a year. SSA calculates the COLA based on the average year-over-year change in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (a form of measuring inflation) for July, August and September. SSI recipients will see the first higher payment on Dec. 31, 2026. Some people receive both SSI and Social Security. Most Social Security recipients will be paid the higher amount starting Jan. 1, 2027. The COLA will also affect Medicare Part B beneficiaries, whose premiums are deducted from their Social Security payments. The 2027 standard premium is projected to rise to $209.50 from $202.90, an increase of $6.60 a month, which would leave the average retired worker about $68 a month better off after COLA. 'Next year's COLA can't come soon enough' SSA Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said the adjustment will give beneficiaries "greater financial stability," and reflects a year of elevated inflation, particularly in gasoline and energy prices. But Nancy Altman, president of the advocacy group Social Security Works, said the increase "doesn't fully account for the costs that Social Security beneficiaries face." Altman said that's because the CPI-W, the inflation index used to calculate Social Security increases, tracks the costs of working people, not retirees, who she said spend a higher share of their income on health care and housing. "Next year's COLA can't come soon enough for many Social Security beneficiaries," she told Yahoo. The Senior Citizens League (TSCL), a nonpartisan seniors' group, was also critical of the payment increase. Executive director Shannon Benton said in a statement that the COLA "falls short of expectations" and that benefits lag behind price spikes because seniors don't see the adjustment until January. It's a concern also shared by beneficiaries. AARP analysis released this week found that 76% of adults 50 and older said a COLA of around 3.5%, slightly lower than the announced figure, would not be enough to help them keep up with rising prices. Kathleen Romig, director of Social Security and disability policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said the annual COLA increase is "especially important in times of high inflation." "This year's COLA is bigger than in many recent years because of rising prices," she told Yahoo. "Another 3.6% … will help beneficiaries keep up with rising costs at the pump and in the grocery store." Some policy groups say the COLA calculation should be updated to use a measure that better reflects retirees' spending habits. The Senior Citizens League wants COLA for retirees to be calculated based on a metric called the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E) . Introduced by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) in 1987, it uses the same underlying price collection system as the main CPI, but instead calculates the market basket to reflect how older Americans actually spend their money , taking a snapshot of retirees' spending priorities as well as how much they spend out of pocket. How do I check if I'm eligible for the increase? You don't need to do anything. The increase is automatic for everyone receiving Social Security or SSI. SSA said enrollees can see their 2027 Medicare Part B premium in their "my Social Security Message Center" starting in late November. Medicare changes will be posted at medicare.gov. Beneficiaries will receive a simplified, one-page COLA notice with their new benefit amount, exact dates and any deductions. Online: People with a personal my Social Security account can view the notice starting in late November, up to three weeks before a mailed notice. People without an account need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by Nov. 18 to see it online. Account holders can also sign up for text or email alerts. By mail: Anyone not enrolled in paperless notices will get theirs in December. For more information, see SSA's COLA page . Key dates Nov. 18: Deadline to create a my Social Security account and enroll in paperless notices to see the notice online. Late November: Online COLA notices will become available to paperless account holders, and Medicare enrollees can see their 2027 Part B premium in their Message Center. The premium is typically deducted directly from monthly Social Security payments. December: Mailed COLA notices go out. Dec. 31, 2026 to January 2027: Beneficiaries begin receiving payments with the increase added. SSI payments normally arrive on the first of the month, but the January payment will arrive on Dec. 31, 2026, because Jan. 1 is a federal holiday. Social Security payments generally go out on the second, third or fourth Wednesday of the month, based on the beneficiary's birthday. People who began receiving Social Security before May 1997, or who receive both Social Security and SSI, generally get their Social Security payment on the third of the month. This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/social-securitys-cola-is-the-biggest-since-2023-americans-will-get-an-extra-75-a-month-on-average-142530711.html

item.title: Is Trump's new press secretary a lawyer? Legal experts are raising doubts.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Katie Zacharia made her debut as President Donald Trump's new White House press secretary Tuesday morning, breaking news (announcing that Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to resign as ambassador to Greece) and sparking commentary about her performance (Trump, for one, said he "thought she was very good"). But Zacharia has also made news, regarding how she has represented herself and her résumé in public appearances. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. "What state did she pass the bar exam in?" a journalist shouted at Trump on Tuesday morning as he walked to Marine One. The president leaned in. Zacharia stood behind him. "She said she's an attorney," the journalist repeated. "Where did she pass the bar exam? Which state?" Trump stepped aside to let Zacharia answer: "When I moved to China," she appeared to say through muffled audio. Journalist Judd Legum, who writes the Popular Information newsletter, identified numerous occasions when Zacharia appeared on national media outlets citing her credentials as a lawyer. He counted 18 appearances on Fox News Channel when she made such mentions, and he found that she also called herself a lawyer on her social media accounts. Zacharia graduated with a law degree from Pepperdine University, but Legum wrote that he could not find that she passed any state's bar exam, which is almost always a requirement for practicing law in the United States. The Washington Post conducted its own review and also could not find any active or expired bar admissions under Zacharia's name, including her maiden name, Black. Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine with a bachelor's degree in 2007 and a law degree in 2011, the university confirmed in an email Tuesday. She then worked as an associate on the international practice team at the law firm Zhong Lun in Beijing, from 2011 until 2013, according to her LinkedIn profile. Her only other legal role was as general counsel of Fix California, a group started by Trump administration official Richard Grenell, from 2024 to 2025. Representatives of Zhong Lun and Fix California did not respond to requests for comment. The White House did not provide evidence that Zacharia has been a licensed lawyer in the United States, but said in a statement that she "worked on international transaction law" in China and "practiced international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials." Several legal ethics experts said that if a person is not a licensed lawyer but is identifying as one, that presents serious ethical and legal problems. "A J.D. degree does not make you a lawyer," said Stephen Gillers, a professor at New York University School of Law. Bruce A. Green, the director of the Louis Stein Center for Law and Ethics at Fordham University School of Law, agreed. "A law school graduate is just that - a law school graduate," he said. A person is considered a lawyer or an attorney only after being admitted to practice law, Green said, adding that in most states, this requires passing a bar exam and demonstrating proper character. Leonard M. Niehoff, a professor at the University of Michigan Law School, said that there is a "world of difference" between having a law degree and being a licensed attorney. And, he said, there could be consequences for falsely claiming to be a licensed attorney. "Many, if not all, states have statutes that prohibit the unauthorized practice of law, which commonly includes falsely holding oneself out as a licensed attorney for purposes of monetary gain," Niehoff said. "Making false or misleading statements about being licensed as an attorney therefore raises not just serious ethical issues but legal ones." Even if Zacharia were licensed in another country, Green said, her public statements in U.S. media would still be misleading if she did not say that she's not licensed in the United States. "Someone in the U.S. who just flat-out calls themselves a lawyer, without further qualification or explanation, will mislead listeners or readers to think that they are permitted to practice law here in the U.S. - which they are not," he said. Zacharia resides in California, according to public records. In a statement Tuesday, a spokesman for the State Bar of California said that it "has no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black having been licensed to practice law in California." The spokesman also said there are no records under Katie, her nickname. The spokesman said that as a general matter, "California Business and Professions section 6126 makes it unlawful for anyone who is not an active licensee of the State Bar, or otherwise authorized pursuant to statute or court rule to practice law in California, to advertise or hold themselves out as practicing or entitled to practice law in California." And even if Zacharia worked for a law firm in China, she probably would not have been admitted to the bar there, given that country's requirements, experts in Chinese law said. "She could not have passed the PRC [People's Republic of China] bar exam, either, since you have to be a PRC national to take it," said Donald C. Clarke, a professor at George Washington University Law School who specializes in Chinese law. Clarke said that firms like Zhong Lun, which he called reputable, can hire foreigners to do certain tasks and can determine whether to require an employee to have passed a foreign bar exam. "But the person still would not be allowed do anything that required a PRC or foreign bar qualification to do," he said, including representing clients in Chinese court. Lester Ross, senior counsel at the law firm WilmerHale, also said the Chinese bar exam is available only to Chinese citizens. "A foreign national who has passed the bar in a foreign jurisdiction may practice the law of such jurisdiction in China and provide his or her understanding of Chinese law, but may not practice Chinese law," he said. Isaac Arnsdorf and Aaron Schaffer contributed to this report. item.title: Trump-appointed judge extends order blocking White House press ban
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A federal judge has extended an order blocking President Donald Trump's administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, broadening his support for the journalists by arguing that the restriction violates their constitutional rights to free speech as well as due process. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him. In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets' Fifth Amendment right to due process. In a late-night ruling Tuesday, he also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump's ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech. Kelly rejected Trump's reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump's stated belief that the outlets' reporting was inaccurate and biased. "Simply put," Kelly wrote, "That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination" — the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like. "Still," he added in his late-night order, "no one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed." But Trump's standoff with the press is far from over. Kelly's order did not address whether Trump can ban the three outlets from the rotating pool of broadcast networks that cover the president in tight spaces and share the reporting. Stepped-up disputes between the president and the press The fight reflects Trump's increasing combativeness against news outlets and reporters whose content he does not like — including sharply curtailing Pentagon access for the press corps that covers the Defense Department. Trump or other parts of the executive branch have also, in policy and in the courts, grappled with The Wall Street Journal, T he Associated Press and The New York Times — in addition to using the FCC to target broadcast networks. The case of the three news outlets is increasingly messy and expensive. After the five-outlet rotating pool stood by CNN and canceled its coverage of Trump, the Justice Department over the weekend announced it was investigating whether those five companies violated antitrust laws in doing so. Kelly's ruling stood largely by the news outlets. He wrote that without a preliminary injunction blocking Trump's ban, the outlets "are likely to suffer irreparable harm, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest tip in their favor." An email to the Justice Department, which is arguing the case on behalf of the administration, was not immediately returned. The White House also did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment. Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the three media organizations, hailed the judge's ruling. "When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said in a statement. "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this 'unconstitutional ban on the free press' for the foreseeable future." Judge says no warning given before banishment Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Trump, previously ordered the White House to restore the reporters' "hard pass" press credentials while he weighed their claims. With that temporary order expiring Tuesday, the judge issued a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo indefinitely while the case is pending. Kelly said that, "to put it mildly," the White House didn't give the plaintiffs any warning that they were in danger of losing their hard passes before Trump's Sept. 18 social media post about their bans. The judge also said the impact of the White House ban goes far beyond a single reporter's ability to do their job. "The ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs' access to the White House press area—a space open to many of their competitors—thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials," the judge wrote. Hard passes give journalists who regularly cover the White House longer term access to its campus without having to get permission ahead of time. The government asked Kelly to suspend his own decision pending an appeal, but the judge said it didn't justify that request. Kelly said the bans impacted a total of 78 reporters at the three news organizations. Earlier judicial action against White House had been only temporary Trump provided no notice before announcing the bans in a Sept. 18 social media post, which criticized their reporting as "fake news." Kelly temporarily blocked the bans on Sept. 24 at the request of the news outlets, which jointly filed a lawsuit in Washington, D.C. Attorneys for the outlets have described Trump's move as "unprecedented and blatantly unconstitutional" under the First and Fifth amendments. They argued that it's illegal for Trump to punish the journalists because he doesn't like the content of their reporting. "The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations — which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable," plaintiffs' lawyers wrote. Government lawyers argued that access to the White House is a privilege — not a right — and said the president can impose the bans to protect national security and to stem the spread of misinformation. "The White House is the official residence and workplace of the President," Justice Department attorneys wrote . "Presidents have had a relationship with the press since the beginning. They have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration." ___ Associated Press reporter Rebecca Boone contributed. item.title: Iran ramps up attacks on ships in bid to keep oil prices high before U.S. midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Parisa Hafezi, Jonathan Saul and Phil Stewart DUBAI/LONDON/WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters. Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel ‌launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort ‌to gain leverage over Washington. Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit. The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using ​different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said. "The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said. The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran's leadership and was fully coordinated across the country's ruling system, the officials said. IRAN USING SPOTTERS A US military official, speaking on condition ‌of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: ⁠after the US destroyed much of Iran's radar capabilities, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official said. Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, ⁠the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said. Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy. The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November's midterm elections, which will decide control ​of ​Congress. US President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the ​vote. The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and ‌extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict. The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic. In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data. There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on October 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization. "There is a tempo increase ‌in strikes, which looks deliberate," one maritime security source said. ATTACKS OVER AN EXPANDED AREA As part of the new strategy, Tehran will ​also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, ​the officials said. Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security ​companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar ‌and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days. The second Iranian official added that ​Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices ​before the November elections. "Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess," the second official said. "Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz." The Pentagon and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. COMPLETE CLOSURE OF HORMUZ SOON, SAYS IRANIAN OFFICIAL Both ​Iranian officials said Tehran is moving towards a situation in which no vessel ‌violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. "It will be complete closure soon," one of the officials said. In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime ​Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained "severe", the second-highest level. "IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, ​and occasional VHF hailing," JMIC said. (Reporting by Parisa Hafezi, Jonathan Saul and Phil Stewart; Editing by Aidan Lewis) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/iran-shifting-tactics-step-attacks-000632093.html

item.title: A mysterious death in Russia renews fears about ancient viruses trapped in Siberia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The unexplained death this month of a Russian lab technician at a Siberian facility for the study of dangerous pathogens raised global anxieties over the potential for an outbreak of pneumonic plague. But while the cause of concern - bound up in a lack of transparency from Moscow - was new, Russia’s frozen hinterlands have long been the source of a separate fear that they could harbor disease risks for which the world is not prepared. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Russian authorities imposed containment measures after the 28-year-old’s death from what they said was pneumonia of “unknown origins,” prompting the United States to ask for more information. A World Health Organization report released Saturday said that Russian authorities found no signs of an outbreak of plague or some other infectious disease, but did not provide sufficient details to identify the origin of the woman’s illness or say whether exposure at work played a role in it. Siberia’s vast wilderness harbors natural reservoirs of pathogens, from fleas that spread plague found in marmots and squirrels to ticks bearing encephalitis to the ancient pathogens frozen in the layer of permafrost. The Russian institute where the lab technician worked was set up in the 1930s as a plague prevention station to curb outbreaks of the deadly bacterial disease that periodically affected local populations as well as people in neighboring Mongolia and China’s Manchuria region. The disease, for which early antibiotic treatments were pioneered that decade, could be spread through contact with marmots, which were hunted for meat and sometimes eaten undercooked or even raw, like in a 2019 case of a Mongolian couple. The settlement of Siberia, which had a 19th-century gold rush and served as a place of exile for criminals under the Russian Empire, connected the remote region to the western parts of the empire and raised the risk of plague spreading farther west, much as epidemic diseases from European Russia, such as cholera and typhus, easily reached Siberia through migrating workers and because of the near-total absence of medical care. A study published this year suggested that the bands of hunter-gatherers who inhabited the Lake Baikal region were the victims of the earliest known plague outbreak, about 5,500 years ago. To this day, plague remains endemic in parts of Siberia and the Russian Far East, where the bacterium persists naturally among wild rodents. Human cases in Russia are rare, however. The country’s last recorded human infection was in 2016, when a 10-year-old boy in the Altai region contracted plague after contact with a marmot. The threat of dangerous disease comes not only from wildlife but also from the millennia-old microbes and viruses stored in the permafrost that underlies the vast majority of the region. About a decade ago, a group of researchers isolated “zombie viruses” from Siberian permafrost, raising fears that a new global medical emergency could be triggered by a disease from the distant past. The permafrost, a dark, cold, oxygenless mass, is a perfect storage container for biological material, and scientists believe that at its deepest levels it may contain viruses up to a million years old, far older than Homo sapiens , the modern human species. In 2023, the researchers - led by Jean-Michel Claverie of Aix-Marseille University in France - published a landmark study in the journal Viruses documenting the revival of ancient viruses from the Siberian permafrost. The report warned that accelerating permafrost thaw caused by climate change poses a potential public health threat by releasing dormant pathogens. Claverie’s team isolated 13 ancient viruses taken from locations across Siberia, belonging to five new viral groups. The oldest, a Pandoravirus yedoma , had been frozen solid beneath an underground lake for 48,500 years, while other, younger strains (around 27,000 years old) were extracted from the remains of a woolly mammoth’s stomach and from mammoth wool. Other researchers have noted that although the revived viruses were able to infect amoebas in lab conditions, it is unclear whether such viruses could infect animals or humans, or find a host outside a controlled laboratory. Claverie and his team cautioned at the time that unknowns remain buried in the permafrost, and a warming climate, which would also open previously untouched lands to deeper development, could expose people to pathogens that affect humans. In 2016, climate change played a role in unleashing anthrax in the remote Yamalo-Nenets region of Siberia, experts said at the time. Unusually high temperatures that summer, soaring to 95 degrees Fahrenheit, melted permafrost, and according to one hypothesis, exposed an infected reindeer carcass. The pathogen spread to living reindeer and eventually to a community of nomadic herders, where a 12-year-old boy died. item.title: Justice Department threatens California over alleged noncitizen voters, letter shows
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jacob Bogage and Andrew Goudsward WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action, according to two letters reviewed by Reuters, part of an unprecedented effort to find evidence ‌of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections. The letters, written by acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter and addressed to California Secretary of State ‌Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan, say the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" ​and were sent mail-in ballots from California. The letters demand that the state and county segregate returned mail-in ballots from voters on the Justice Department's list and not tabulate their votes "until citizenship has been determined." In cases where ballots have not been sent out yet, it orders California officials to withhold them from those on the list until their citizenship is confirmed. The federal government "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," according to the letters, if state and county officials do not follow its instructions. "Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes," ‌McCotter wrote. The letters mark an escalation of the Trump administration's ⁠attempts to pressure states over alleged voting by non-US citizens and signal the Justice Department may be prepared to challenge ballots in the weeks leading up to the November 3 election, when Republicans will be defending their narrow majorities in Congress. Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten ⁠Pels confirmed the existence of the letters in a statement to Reuters, adding: "The department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law.” Representatives from the White House and the California secretary of state's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Logan also did not immediately respond. FRAUD CLAIMS The Justice Department under President Donald Trump ​has ​repeatedly claimed that voting by non-US citizens is widespread, despite multiple studies showing it is rare. Though ​states may have added more than 30,000 noncitizens to their voter ‌rolls since 2000 due to software glitches and clerical errors, Reuters found in September, it was unclear how many had cast a ballot. Experts said the numbers were too small relative to the country’s 170 million registered voters to affect elections. In July, the Justice Department sent letters to chief election officials in all 50 states warning they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls or cast ballots. The department's Civil Rights Division has demanded nonpublic voter data, including voters' Social Security numbers or dates of birth, from nearly all states as part of its hunt for noncitizens on state rolls. It has sued 30 Democratic- and Republican-led states that ‌refused to hand over their rolls, but has lost 26 of those cases without winning one. Reuters reported ​last month that the Department of Homeland Security was using a commercial data broker to find sensitive ​voter information not included in publicly available rolls, which officials and experts ​warned could lead to citizens being falsely flagged as illegal voters and potentially detained. Federal prosecutors have also ramped up prosecutions of noncitizens ‌for allegedly voting in past elections or submitting fraudulent registrations, touting 16 ​new criminal cases on Monday. Officials in Democratic-led ​California have tussled for months with the Trump administration over its attempts to intervene in election procedures over allegations of voter fraud. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed California officials on July 16 that the federal government believed the state had noncitizens on its voting rolls, according to the letter. California could prove pivotal in ​deciding control of the US House of Representatives, especially after ‌the state's voters approved a new congressional map that heavily favors Democrats as part of a nationwide redistricting sprint that began in Republican-led states. Voters in ​Los Angeles will also weigh in on a ballot measure that would allow certain noncitizen legal residents to cast ballots in municipal elections. (Reporting by Jacob Bogage ​and Andrew Goudsward in Washington; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage, Jamie Freed and Daniel Wallis) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/exclusive-us-justice-department-threatens-034849746.html

item.title: Major U.S. banks turned away customers over political and religious views, report says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Comptroller of the Currency says the nation's nine largest banks denied financial services to customers based on their political, religious, or social beliefs, according to a regulatory review released Wednesday. The OCC reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints and received approximately 50,000 documents from JPMorgan Chase Bank, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo Bank, U.S. Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank, and BMO Bank regarding their policies, procedures, practices, and individual customer decisions. The federal banking watchdog determined that the banks' sweeping internal guidelines lacked objective, risk-based criteria, effectively shutting out legitimate customers and businesses based on ideological leanings rather than financial risk. The OCC said its findings reveal a systematic effort within the banking sector to restrict access for politically sensitive industries through both public and nonpublic policies. Federal regulators found that lenders restricted certain sectors' access to financial services, including oil and gas exploration; coal mining; firearms or ammunition manufacturing or distribution; construction or operation of detention facilities; and the manufacturing, distribution or online retail of tobacco or e-cigarettes. The Trump administration has voiced growing concerns over "de-banking" and the use of the financial system to achieve social and political objectives. "Today's report provides irrefutable evidence that the nation's largest banks have denied, debanked, and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses," said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould. "Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations, or political views. " All nine banks report having reassessed the role of reputation risk in decisions to accept or terminate new customers, according to the OCC's report. Several banks said they had minimized reliance on reputation risk, and bank employees now must consider it in the context of other financial or business consequences, including credit risk, money laundering and terrorist financing risk. The Bank Policy Institute, a lobbying group that represents the banks, said in a statement in reaction to the report, "We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk and rather than reputational risk." The group also noted it would continue to work with the administration and Congress on proposals that ensure that political or religious beliefs do not unfairly affect customers' access to banking services. JPMorgan Chase said in a statement, "We take this seriously, learned from it, and improved the way we do business. We agree with the Administration on a broader point: years of operating in a regulatory environment that often second-guessed decisions contributed to a culture of caution across the banking industry. That system needs fixing." The bank says its policies prohibit discrimination against customers based on political or religious views. A spokesperson for Wells Fargo and Citigroup declined to comment on the OCC's report, while PNC said it was reviewing the findings. Bank of America, U.S. Bank and Capital One had not responded for comment as of this writing. The review was directed by President Trump's executive order, "Guaranteeing Fair Access to Banking for All Americans," to determine whether these banks' policies or practices required or influenced banks to deny or limit access to financial services to Americans because of their political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities. The OCC is considering further actions and writing new rules to prevent banks from discriminating against customers or prospective customers based on their political or religious beliefs. The OCC is also coordinating its debanking review with the reviews of other federal and state partners. "Notwithstanding certain efforts by the largest banks to rein in these practices, I am not confident that they will be enough," said Gould. Jennifer Schonberger is a veteran financial journalist covering markets, the economy, and investing. At Yahoo Finance, she covers the Federal Reserve, Congress, the White House, the Treasury, the SEC, the economy, cryptocurrencies, and the intersection of Washington policy with finance. Follow her on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram . David Hollerith is a senior reporter at Yahoo Finance covering the cryptocurrency and stock markets. Follow him on X at @DsHollers . item.title: Trump's meme coin has lost 95% of its value. Buyers still want a seat at his table.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
More than half of the top holders listed as competing for seats at President Trump's next meme coin dinner have used cryptocurrency exchanges that prohibit U.S. customers, indicating that many of the buyers are based overseas, according to a CBS News analysis. The gala, set for Nov. 22 at the Trump National Golf Club outside Washington, D.C., will seat the 185 largest holders of the $TRUMP meme coin, according to the website for Fight Fight Fight LLC, the company behind the coin. A public leaderboard for the event only lists the top 100 holders. Mr. Trump is billed as the featured speaker alongside three yet-to-be-named "legends." The top 29 holders will get upfront seating and a VIP reception with the president, the website says. The upcoming dinner is the latest example of the unprecedented intermingling of business and politics during Mr. Trump's second term. Mr. Trump earned at least $635 million in royalties last year from a licensing deal tied to the $TRUMP token, according to his financial disclosure . Mr. Trump stands to earn more money from the coin, since an affiliate of the Trump Organization earns revenue whenever the coin is traded, according to the meme coin's website . "Foreign actors used to need a back door to try to influence a president," said Zach Everson, a researcher for the progressive consumer rights advocacy group Public Citizen. "Trump is holding the front door open and inviting them in for a steak dinner." Out of the 100 top holders listed as competing for seats, at least 52 moved funds through crypto exchanges that bar U.S. customers, including Binance, Bybit and MEXC, according to the CBS News analysis. Because exchanges like Binance bar U.S. customers, analysts typically treat accounts that use them as likely belonging to people outside the U.S., said Matt Fiebach, co-founder of the crypto data firm Entropy Advisors. "All you can know with certainty is that a non-U.S. person or entity sent funds," Fiebach said. A cryptocurrency exchange is a company, much like a stock brokerage, where customers trade dollars or other currencies for crypto. CIC Digital LLC, a Trump Organization affiliate, and another company, Fight Fight Fight, together own 80% of the total $TRUMP supply, according to the project's website. The parent company of Fight Fight Fight, Celebration Cards LLC, uses Mr. Trump's name and likeness under a licensing agreement, the website adds. At least 44 of the users on the leaderboard transacted through Binance prior to purchasing $TRUMP, the analysis found. CBS News examined the transaction histories of the crypto wallets listed on the gala leaderboard using data from the blockchain intelligence firm Arkham. While it's not possible to see who owns specific wallets, it is possible to identify which exchanges are being used to purchase crypto tokens. The users that transacted on the exchanges that bar U.S. customers account for nearly $6.8 million of the more than $15 million in value reflected on the coin leaderboard as of Wednesday. A meme coin is a type of asset that is typically used for commemorative purposes or comedic value, and not a currency. In 2023, Binance was forced to offload its U.S. customers after it pleaded guilty to federal charges that included failure to prevent money laundering on its platform and sanctions violations. Its co-founder, Changpeng Zhao, also pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program. (Mr. Trump granted a pardon to Zhao in October 2025, claiming the crypto billionaire was a victim of a political prosecution under President Biden). Exchanges can also shed light on who might be making moves to sell their tokens. The largest holder of $TRUMP moved about $70 million worth of the coin in September to an account where it could be sold, just before the gala dinner contest was announced, The Washington Sun reported . The coin's total market value has dropped more than 95% since its peak in January 2025, to about $532 million, data show. Democrats and progressive watchdog groups have raised foreign influence questions about the $TRUMP coin, warning that people overseas could be paying for access to the president. While it may be possible for a U.S.-based user to circumvent foreign exchange prohibitions by masking their location using a virtual private network, or VPN, many exchanges say they take measures intended to prevent this. The Trump Organization did not respond to requests for comment. A White House official said in a statement that the Trump administration only acts in the "best interest of the American people." The official added that the meme coin event is "a private event, not a government function, and there is no promise of official government action in exchange for attending." This wouldn't be the first time the president has headlined a $TRUMP coin gala. Mr. Trump appeared at a similar meme coin dinner in May 2025 at his golf club in Virginia, and another this April at his Mar-a-Lago resort. The meme coin has been a financial boon to Mr. Trump, who raked in more than $1.4 billion last year from crypto-related ventures, according to his financial disclosure . The current top spot on the Trump gala leaderboard is occupied by a wallet that holds about 1.5 million $TRUMP tokens, valued at nearly $3 million. That wallet received its $TRUMP holdings in two transfers on Oct. 8 — the largest of which came from another wallet that has used the Binance exchange. It's unclear whether the same person controls both. "As was the case with Trump's previous meme coin gala, it appears that the majority of $TRUMP investors are purchasing his meme coin through overseas exchanges," said Virginia Canter, who worked as an ethics lawyer in Republican and Democratic presidential administrations. "Foreign actors are literally buying a seat at the president's own table." Within days of its January 2025 launch, the Trump token reached a peak value of $75.35. It has since fallen dramatically — to roughly $2 as of Wednesday. The sharp decline in value has led Democrats to call it an alleged "pump-and-dump" scheme. Mr. Trump's ties to crypto are expected to be a top oversight area for Democrats should they take a majority in the House or Senate in the 2026 midterm elections. The Trump family co-founded and holds a stake in World Liberty Financial, a separate crypto company launched in 2024. It generated hundreds of millions in revenue for Mr. Trump last year, his financial disclosure shows . World Liberty Financial drew scrutiny in 2025 after MGX, an investment firm backed by the Abu Dhabi government, used World Liberty's stablecoin to make a $2 billion investment in Binance. Both Binance and Mr. Trump denied the pardon for Zhao, the Binance co-founder, was connected to the transaction. "I don't know who he is," Mr. Trump told CBS News days after pardoning the crypto billionaire. item.title: Netflix cuts 1,000 jobs in its biggest layoffs ever despite soaring profits
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Netflix is swinging the axe — laying off around 1,000 employees, representing 6% of its workforce, in what is its biggest layoff to date. Most of the layoffs will affect workers in Netflix’s product, technology, legal and HR teams, co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in an email to employees Wednesday morning about the layoffs. More from Variety How AI Is Used by Netflix at Its VFX Eyeline Studios, Revealed by VP Mohsen Mousavi at View Conference Netflix Scores Exclusive 2030 FIFA World Cup Rights in Spain and Andorra in Landmark Deal Appetite for Agatha Christie Shows No Signs of Slowing 50 Years After Her Death: 'She Has Such Enduring Appeal' “Our mission — to entertain the world — is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” the co-CEOs said in the memo, a copy of which was obtained by Variety (read it in full below). A Netflix spokesperson said the company did not have any comment beyond the memo from Sarandos and Peters. Netflix, the industry’s biggest premium streaming provider with more than 325 million customers globally, has posted double-digit growth in both revenue and profits in recent years. In 2025, the company had $45.2 billion in revenue (up 16%) and net income of $11 billion (up 26%). “Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast,” Sarandos and Peters said in the memo. The co-CEOs continued, “We’ll continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation.” However, they said, “Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors.” As of the end of 2025, Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees. The last major Netflix layoffs came in 2022, when it axed about 450 staffers following the streamer’s net decline of 200,000 subscribers in the first quarter of that year, its first such drop in more than a decade. The company has made additional smaller cutbacks since then, including letting go several dozen members of its global product team earlier in 2026. Netflix is scheduled to report third quarter 2026 earnings on Tuesday, Oct. 20, after market close. For the second quarter, the streamer posted earnings in line with Wall Street forecasts but issued Q3 revenue guidance below analyst expectations, driving the stock price down. item.title: Trump administration delays IRS data that could show who benefited from GOP tax cuts
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration is delaying the release of detailed data showing how Republicans’ 2025 tax cuts affected millions of Americans’ taxes, even as it tries to sell voters on the law ahead of the midterm elections. The numbers document which tax breaks were claimed by people in different income brackets, as well as information like how much they paid in taxes. The IRS typically releases the data in the wake of each filing season, and this year's rollout is more anticipated because it’s expected to provide the first detailed look at how taxpayers are taking advantage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including its new deductions for overtime wages and tipped income. The data was scheduled to be released in July, and then updated again in September, as the IRS processed more people’s returns —but the agency hasn't published either. The IRS said it is awaiting approval from the Treasury Department to publish the figures. But the delay has already irked some who complain it is part of a pattern of the administration withholding otherwise routine releases of tax data. “I think they are hiding stuff that doesn’t line up with all the crowing the CEO has been doing,” Nina Olson, a former national taxpayer advocate, said of Frank Bisignano, the IRS's day-to-day leader who has joined Republican lawmakers in touting the breaks to voters. The lack of detailed numbers on the 2026 filing season comes as the agency is also under fire for withholding a periodic report on the so-called tax gap, which is the share of taxes owed but not yet paid. The administration declined to answer questions about the delay on the record. In an emailed statement, an official speaking on condition of anonymity said its “priority is to release accurate and reliable data” following “major changes” to the tax code. The official did not say when the figures might be released. During the filing season, the IRS publishes weekly top-line statistics documenting how many returns it processed, how many refunds it issued and how much money taxpayers typically got back — figures the administration hyped earlier this year as evidence of the benefits of their tax cuts. But the delayed data is far more granular, showing the uptake of individual provisions in the code as well as things like how much more people in different income groups reported earning, and how many people still owed money to the IRS at the time of filing. In past years, the figures have created problems for the majority party when they didn’t show what lawmakers hoped for. Republicans took heat when the figures released the first year after their 2017 tax cuts showed fewer people taking deductions for charitable contributions, for example. It’s possible this year’s figures include less-than-flattering details about Republicans’ tax cuts — they could show the tax burden shifting between income groups, for instance, or a suspicious number of people claiming specific breaks, said Barry Johnson, a former top IRS official. But the reason why the data isn't out yet could also be more mundane, like if an unusual number of people requested filing extensions. “There’s all sorts of things it could be — you can’t know until you see the data whether it’s they don’t like the answers, or whether the data themselves really aren’t useful,” said Johnson, who was the IRS’s director of Statistics of Income from 2014 to 2025. But the Treasury isn’t supposed to be blocking the release of the figures, he said, pointing to a law Trump signed in his first term that gave statistical agencies, like at the IRS, more power to decide when to publish data. “By law, the IRS determines what they release and when it gets released,” said Johnson. “Treasury shouldn’t have a role in determining the timing of any statistical release. “It’s unusual,” he said. “It would telling to see if everything comes out in the middle of November, and then the stories a little bit challenging, then you’d say it was being held up to get past the midterms.” The first batch of data, showing figures through May, was originally slated for release in July, but is now listed on the IRS's website as “pending.” The update with numbers through July was slated to go out Sept. 17. The figures, when they're finally released, won’t be the final word on this filing season because they don’t include people who asked for filing extensions and now face an Oct. 15 deadline for completing their returns. Those taxpayers tend to be wealthier, so they tend to be understated in the figures. The mid-July data typically covers 95% of taxpayers, 87% of the income reported and 82% of the taxes paid, the IRS says.
